project-charter.title: Understand the Bench Vice Power-Screw Application

cards.title: Engineering Brief — Bench Vice Power-Screw Design
cards.body: A workshop bench vice is a fundamental mechanical clamping device. You are required to analyse the power-screw mechanism of a conventional bench vice, estimate the total torque an operator must apply to the handle to generate a specified clamping load, determine the mechanical efficiency of the screw mechanism, and assess whether the screw is self-locking under the given friction conditions.

cards.title: Power Screw — Rotary Input to Axial Output
cards.body:
A power screw converts rotational motion into controlled linear motion and force.

In a bench vice:
  Handle rotation → Screw rotation about its longitudinal axis
  Screw rotation → Helical thread interaction between screw and nut (fixed body)
  Thread interaction → Axial translation of the movable jaw
  Jaw translation → Clamping force on the workpiece

The screw must overcome two distinct friction interfaces:
  1. Thread Friction — resistance at the helical thread engagement between screw and nut
  2. Collar Friction — resistance at the thrust collar interface between the screw head and the movable jaw

For a square-thread power screw, the torque to raise the load (generate clamping force) is:
  T_s = (W × dm / 2) × [(μ + tan α) / (1 − μ × tan α)]

where:
  W   = clamping load (N)
  dm  = mean screw diameter (mm)
  μ   = coefficient of thread friction (dimensionless)
  α   = helix angle (degrees)

College friction torque:
  T_c = μc × W × dc / 2

Total operating torque:
  T = T_s + T_c

Mechanical efficiency of the screw:
  η (%) = [W × L / (2π × T)] × 100

Self-locking condition (screw will not back-drive under load):
  μ > tan α

cards.title: Engineering Objectives
items: Identify the bench vice power-screw components from Engineering Asset EA-18.
Trace the load path from handle rotation through thread interaction to clamping force.
Establish all given design data for the bench vice screw mechanism.
Calculate mean screw diameter and helix angle.
Compute thread friction torque using the square-thread torque equation.
Account for collar friction and determine total operating torque.
Calculate power-screw efficiency and verify the self-locking condition.
Estimate the required operator hand force at the handle.
Provide a technically justified engineering judgement on the mechanism suitability.

component-identification.title: Identify Bench Vice Components and Mechanical Functions
component-identification.description: Engineering asset illustrating the conventional bench vice power-screw mechanism with labelled components, force arrows, and friction interfaces.

labels.feedback: The fixed jaw is integral with the vice body and remains stationary during clamping operations.
The movable jaw slides horizontally along the guide rails toward or away from the fixed jaw under the action of the power screw.
Hardened steel jaw plates are bolted to both jaw faces and provide the direct clamping contact surface with the workpiece.
The workpiece is the component being held between the two opposing jaw plates during machining or assembly operations.
The horizontal power screw converts the rotary torque applied by the operator at the handle into axial clamping force on the movable jaw.
The screw head is the enlarged end of the power screw through which the sliding handle is inserted. It transmits handle torque to the screw.
The sliding tommy-bar handle passes through the screw head perpendicular to the screw axis. Operator pushes the handle tangentially to rotate the screw.
The threaded engagement zone is where the helical thread of the power screw meshes with the internal threaded nut in the fixed vice body, converting rotation to axial force.
The sliding guide rails support and constrain the movable jaw to translate strictly in the horizontal direction, preventing rotation or tilting.
The fixed cast-iron vice body houses the threaded nut, provides the mounting base, and supports the entire mechanism.

motion-sequence.title: Understand Rotary-to-Linear Motion and Load Path
motion-sequence.prompt: Analyse how the operator's hand effort at the handle is ultimately converted into clamping force on the workpiece, referring to Engineering Asset EA-18.

mcq.question: Which sequence correctly describes the complete mechanical load transmission path from operator input to clamping force in a bench vice power-screw mechanism?

options.label: Operator applies tangential force on handle → Handle lever arm applies torque to screw head → Screw rotates about its longitudinal axis → Helical thread interaction with fixed nut converts rotation to axial thrust → Axial thrust drives movable jaw toward fixed jaw → Movable jaw plate applies clamping force on workpiece
Operator pulls movable jaw directly → Clamping force is applied → Handle rotates as a result → Screw tightens afterward
Fixed jaw moves toward workpiece → Screw pushes fixed jaw → Handle is rotated by screw → Workpiece is compressed from both sides simultaneously
Workpiece deformation drives jaw movement → Jaw movement rotates screw → Screw rotation requires no external handle torque

design-data.title: Establish Design Data for the Power-Screw Mechanism
design-data.prompt: Before beginning calculations, confirm all design parameters for the bench vice screw mechanism. All values are as specified in the engineering brief.

mcq.question: Which set of design parameters correctly represents the complete given data for the EA-18 bench vice power-screw mechanism?

options.label: Clamping load W = 20,000 N | Nominal screw diameter d = 24 mm | Single-start square thread pitch p = 5 mm | Lead L = p = 5 mm | Thread friction coefficient μ = 0.12 | Mean collar diameter dc = 36 mm | Collar friction coefficient μc = 0.10 | Effective handle radius R = 200 mm
Clamping load W = 20,000 N | Nominal screw diameter d = 30 mm | Multi-start thread lead L = 15 mm | Thread friction μ = 0.20 | Collar diameter dc = 50 mm | Handle radius R = 150 mm
Clamping load W = 10,000 N | d = 24 mm | p = 5 mm | L = 10 mm (double-start) | μ = 0.12 | dc = 36 mm | μc = 0.10 | R = 200 mm
Clamping load W = 20,000 N | d = 24 mm | p = 8 mm | L = 8 mm | μ = 0.08 | dc = 24 mm | μc = 0.08 | R = 100 mm

mean-diameter-helix.title: Determine Mean Diameter and Helix Angle
mean-diameter-helix.prompt:
For a square-thread power screw:
  Mean Screw Diameter:  dₘ = d − (p / 2)
  Helix Angle:          tan α = L / (π · dₘ)

Given Data:
  Nominal Diameter (d) = 24 mm
  Thread Pitch (p)     = 5 mm
  Screw Lead (L)       = p = 5 mm  (Single-Start Square Thread)

Calculate the mean screw diameter (dₘ) and helix angle (α).

mcq.question: What are the correct mean screw diameter (dₘ) and helix angle (α) for the bench vice power screw?

options.label: dₘ = d = 24.0 mm  (assumed mean diameter = nominal diameter)  |  tan α = L / (π · d) = 5 / (π × 24) = 0.06631  |  α ≈ 3.79°

thread-torque.title: Calculate Thread Friction Torque
thread-torque.prompt:
For a square-thread power screw, the torque required to raise the clamping load (overcome thread friction and generate axial force) is given by:

  Tₛ = (W · dₘ / 2) · [ (μ + tan α) / (1 − μ · tan α) ]

where:
  W     = 20,000 N       (Clamping Load)
  dₘ    = 21.5 mm        (Mean Screw Diameter)
  μ     = 0.12           (Thread Friction Coefficient)
  α     ≈ 4.23°          (Helix Angle)
  tan α ≈ 0.07402

Calculate the friction angle φ = tan⁻¹(μ) and thread friction torque Tₛ.
Express the result in N·mm.

mcq.question: What is the correct thread friction torque Tₛ for the bench vice screw mechanism?

options.label: Tₛ = W · dₘ · μ = 20,000 × 21.5 × 0.12 = 51,600 N·mm  (friction force only — helix angle α ignored; omits the (μ + tan α)/(1 − μ tan α) correction)
Tₛ = (W · dₘ / 2) · tan α = (20,000 × 21.5 / 2) × 0.07402 = 215,000 × 0.07402 = 15,914 N·mm  (load component only — thread friction μ ignored)
Tₛ = (W · L) / (2π) = (20,000 × 5) / (2π) = 100,000 / 6.2832 ≈ 15,915 N·mm  (ideal screw torque without friction)

collar-total-torque.title: Account for Collar Friction and Total Operating Torque
collar-total-torque.prompt:
Collar friction torque accounts for friction at the thrust collar interface between the screw head and the movable jaw:

  T_c = μ_c · W · (d_c / 2)

where:
  μ_c  = 0.10     (Collar Friction Coefficient)
  W    = 20,000 N (Clamping Load)
  d_c  = 36 mm    (Mean Collar Diameter)

Total operating torque required at the handle:

  T = Tₛ + T_c

Use Tₛ ≈ 42,088 N·mm from the previous activity.
Express results in N·mm and N·m.

mcq.question: What are the correct collar friction torque (T_c) and total operating torque (T), expressed in N·mm and N·m?

efficiency-selflocking.title: Calculate Efficiency, Self-Locking Condition and Operator Force
efficiency-selflocking.prompt:
1. Power-Screw Mechanical Efficiency:
   η (%) = [ (W · L) / (2π · T) ] × 100%

2. Self-Locking Condition:
   Screw is self-locking (will not back-drive under clamping load) if:
   μ > tan α   (or friction angle φ > helix angle α)

3. Required Operator Hand Force at Handle:
   F = T / R

Given:
  W = 20,000 N,   L = 5 mm,   T ≈ 78,088 N·mm,   R = 200 mm
  μ = 0.12,   tan α ≈ 0.07402  (α ≈ 4.23°)

mcq.question: What are the correct efficiency (η), self-locking assessment, and required operator hand force (F)?

options.label: η = [ (W · L) / T ] × 100% = (100,000 / 78,088) × 100% ≈ 128.06%  (forgot 2π in denominator)  |  Self-Locking: NOT self-locking  |  F = T / R = 78,088 / 200 = 390.4 N
η = (Tₛ / T) × 100% = (42,088 / 78,088) × 100% ≈ 53.90%  (this is thread torque fraction, not overall efficiency)  |  Self-Locking: YES  |  F = 390.0 N

options.title: MECHANISM IS SUITABLE — SELF-LOCKING CONFIRMED, OPERATOR FORCE WITHIN PRACTICAL RANGE
options.description: The bench vice mechanism is self-locking (μ = 0.12 > tan α ≈ 0.074), which ensures the screw will not back-drive under clamping load — a critical safety requirement. The calculated efficiency of approximately 20% is typical for conventional square-thread power screws, where friction is deliberately maintained to ensure self-locking. An operator hand force of approximately 390 N at R = 200 mm handle is within the practical operating range for a workshop bench vice. The mechanism is engineeringly suitable for the specified 20 kN clamping requirement.

options.title: MECHANISM REQUIRES IMPROVEMENT — LOW EFFICIENCY AND ELEVATED OPERATOR EFFORT
options.description: While the mechanism is self-locking, efficiency of approximately 20% indicates significant friction losses, with collar friction alone accounting for approximately 36,000 N·mm out of 78,088 N·mm total torque (46% of total losses). Potential improvements include: (1) Increasing handle radius beyond 200 mm to reduce operator hand force; (2) Introducing a thrust bearing at the collar interface to reduce μc from 0.10; (3) Considering ACME thread profile for improved efficiency while retaining adequate self-locking; (4) Applying appropriate lubrication to both thread and collar interfaces. The design choice depends on whether minimizing operator effort or maintaining simplicity and reliability is the primary priority.
